# The History of Astrophysics
**Our understanding of space before technology**
### _By Angus_

### Distance to the Moon

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701591-8593d947-effa-47ff-880f-a29a998d4533.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQwNzcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5Mzc3NywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxNTkxLTg1OTNkOTQ3LWVmZmEtNDdmZi04ODBmLWEyOWE5OThkNDUzMy5wbmc_.xo7mLbKmBYDtzdHrfnbsLsGpbAEAT4MFxd286po1TZ4" width="20%">

In 270BC, **Aristarchus of Samos** was able to calculate the distance between the Earth and the Moon.

During a **total lunar eclipse**, which happens every 2 to 3 years, the moon passes through the Earth’s shadow, called the **umbra**. Aristarchus measured how much time the Moon was in the Earth’s shadow during a lunar eclipse and found it to be around 192 minutes or 3.2 hours.
<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701652-7402bbb1-7846-46d6-9d6e-e273a05e3f6a.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxNjUyLTc0MDJiYmIxLTc4NDYtNDZkNi05ZDZlLWUyNzNhMDVlM2Y2YS5wbmc_.Ey-N5kPeuorLeCSYsibw9GAUpW4n7O4gw921MAXSQJk" width="50%">

Working with the assumption that the Sun’s rays are uniform, he figured that **the umbra was twice the radius of the Earth.** Taking into account that for a circular lunar orbit, the Moon’s speed is constant relative to the Earth, he made this ratio (as shown below), stating that **the speed of the moon throughout its whole orbit is the same as the speed of the moon over the course of a lunar eclipse **(which we now know isn’t true as the Moon’s orbit is elliptical so its orbital speed varies). He wrote the speeds down in terms of the distances and times of the entire orbit and the portion of the orbit which took place during the eclipse, where R is the distance between the Earth and the Moon, and r is the radius of the Earth. Using this, he calculated that the radius of the Moon’s orbit (its distance from the Earth) was around **65x** the Earth’s radius.

The distance is actually **60x** the radius of the Earth, which isn’t very far off!

Of course, the Sun’s rays don’t form a shadow like this, in fact it is more conical, therefore the assumption that the umbra is 2r wide is too high. Also, the Moon does nor orbit the Earth on the same plane to which the Earth orbits the Sun, meaning that the distance travelled by the Moon within the umbra is less that 2r, so this would be why Aristarchus’ estimate was too high.

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701691-5febc847-b7e7-4007-b750-4c66278d5528.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxNjkxLTVmZWJjODQ3LWI3ZTctNDAwNy1iNzUwLTRjNjYyNzhkNTUyOC5wbmc_.35j62mIsRaVZ4y68AF3oUVxaixDgHt--MT3-esVAFYA" width="50%"><img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701727-2b316338-e781-4451-b06f-b0b769cbb095.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxNzI3LTJiMzE2MzM4LWU3ODEtNDQ1MS1iMDZmLWIwYjc2OWNiYjA5NS5wbmc_.Tt13HInRfRksL_7hl6l1X9B9LpmYCumw7ebnEco8YPY" width="50%">
<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701757-15f04bb8-4cb8-4399-8ab9-bfc157d7c1fa.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxNzU3LTE1ZjA0YmI4LTRjYjgtNDM5OS04YWI5LWJmYzE1N2Q3YzFmYS5wbmc_.wS0xr-miEon4izN6K1ZydWrUVBv14-WAXKqOH52sjLs" width="50%">

### Earth's circumference

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701922-acb75c44-a9c7-4d19-9254-ae804d2c5d8e.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxOTIyLWFjYjc1YzQ0LWE5YzctNGQxOS05MjU0LWFlODA0ZDJjNWQ4ZS5wbmc_.kOkKPncTW4ALWI1OajSi3l8mq5NCgll7rW9ZmEkOX7k" width="30%">

In 240BC, **Eratosthenes** learned that in a town called Syene, there were **no shadows at noon on the longest day of the year**, but on the same day in Alexandria, there were small shadows.

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701989-cc0aab9a-6a92-427b-96ca-606eab06f716.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxOTg5LWNjMGFhYjlhLTZhOTItNDI3Yi05NmNhLTYwNmVhYjA2ZjcxNi5wbmc_.AHruOKmjYYA_G0NWZhUwybN4Yyb7b_IL51R6Es74S40" width="50%">

For there to be no shadows in Syene on this day, the Sun must have been **directly overhead.**

Eratosthenes measured the shadow produced by a vertical stick in the ground in Alexandria and found that the angle of the shadow produced therefore the incident sunlight was **7°** to the vertical, and if there is no shadow in Syene, the angle is **0°**. Eratosthenes deduced that Alexandria was tilted by 7° relative to Syene, therefore the angle of the sector between the centre of the Earth and the two towns must be 7°.

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702021-b11dd270-579e-435c-90d1-a5d0757dae6d.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyMDIxLWIxMWRkMjcwLTU3OWUtNDM1Yy05MGQxLWE1ZDA3NTdkYWU2ZC5wbmc_.DOjx9jdPhQlznji9gfuqBAvndIp2qM58w1aIjFO-wKg" width="20%">
<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552701949-854e830b-ea4d-433a-b8d6-8c916fbe3212.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAxOTQ5LTg1NGU4MzBiLWVhNGQtNDMzYS1iOGQ2LThjOTE2ZmJlMzIxMi5wbmc_.0om27MPLtewj81kQLi3VOKj1rysg7oIJPRzGEdzVoaI" width="50%">

Eratosthenes hired a bematist to measure the distance between the two cities, and he returned with the figure **780km.** He then figured that the **ratio of the angle of the sector and 360°** should be the **same** as the **ratio of the length of the arc(the distance between the cities) and the circumference of the Earth.** Using this calculation, he found that the radius of the Earth is **6370km**, and the actual value is **6371km.**


### Distance to the Sun

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702113-c4f10d3e-8040-4506-b76f-0ed0c3f84656.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyMTEzLWM0ZjEwZDNlLTgwNDAtNDUwNi1iNzZmLTBlZDBjM2Y4NDY1Ni5wbmc_.hKP1Otn-6fEjo4HUond7itb22AzszC8CTl3MpQwgHY8" width="20%">

In 270BC, **Aristarchus of Samos** was able to find the distance between the Earth and the Sun.

During a half-moon, **half** of the visible surface of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun. Through this, Aristarchus drew this **right-angled triangle**:

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702282-cc48d0b6-edfd-4d5b-9592-445ca36f17d0.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQzMjAsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDAyMCwicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyMjgyLWNjNDhkMGI2LWVkZmQtNGQ1Yi05NTkyLTQ0NWNhMzZmMTdkMC5wbmc_.pzk1PbV830uVNpMs5JUYONtvxP7txCLeiMW9pr5RVEA" width="75%">

cosθ = adj/hyp

1/cosθ = hyp/adj, or R/r

He found that θ = 87°, so found that the distance between the Sun and the Earth was 20x the distance between the Moon and the Earth.

However, the actual angle was around 89.5°, giving a ratio of 400:1.

Both the Sun and the Moon have a similar angular size of 0.5°, meaning that they are about the same size in the sky, but as the Sun is 400x further than the Moon, it follows that the Sun is also 400x wider than the Moon.

He was also the first person to propose the heliocentric model of the Solar System, and used the idea of the Sun’s large size relative to the Earth’s to prove his ideas.


### Distance to the Moon using parallax

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702505-98d7f460-8bf0-4416-a9b2-8002d0b9fa77.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQ3MDcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDQwNywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyNTA1LTk4ZDdmNDYwLThiZjAtNDQxNi1hOWIyLTgwMDJkMGI5ZmE3Ny5wbmc_.s2vszHNU9AbTVFtGMECNJQ7YBeKgg5AXEu_ZynisbQw" width="20%">

In 190BC, **Hipparchus** used a different method to calculate the distance to the Moon. There was a **solar eclipse**, which is when the **Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth**, causing the Sun to be obstructed by the Moon. In a city in Turkey called Hellespont (with a latitude of 41°), the eclipse had reached **totality**, meaning that the Moon passed directly in front of the Sun. However, in Alexandria (of latitude 31°), Hipparchus observed that a small part of the Sun was still visible (about **1/5** of its diameter).

Since the Sun is 400x larger than the Moon and the Moon is 400x closer than the Sun, they both have a similar **angular size** of about **0.5°**.

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702538-bc0801b5-ebe1-4e89-aa6b-6aac28dd26af.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQ3MDcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDQwNywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyNTM4LWJjMDgwMWI1LWViZTEtNGU4OS1hYTZiLTZhYWMyOGRkMjZhZi5wbmc_.a7BpdczgZ7u7uiYuRB7I8qDj2ETv3nNCHdBu11vrbPY" width="75%">

1/5 x 0.5 =0.1°, this is the **parallax angle**, which is the angle formed by the Moon and the two cities on Earth.

The **latitude difference** between the two cities is **10°**.

Distance between cities' latitudes = 2πr x 10°/360°, where r is the **Earth’s radius.** You can also express this **same distance** by drawing a circle centred from the Moon. Distance between two cities = 2πR x 0.1°/360°, where R is the **radius of the Moon’s orbit.**

These two expressions are equal, and solving them gives the ratio of R:r as **100:1.**

However, this is not completely correct as it assumes that the Moon is **directly overhead.** After correcting this, he found a value of around **63** Earth radii, which is very close to the current value of **60.**

### Precession (axial wobble)
<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702644-89f1c6b0-a051-4bb9-84df-decfba642a32.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQ3MDcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDQwNywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyNjQ0LTg5ZjFjNmIwLWEwNTEtNGJiOS04NGRmLWRlY2ZiYTY0MmEzMi5wbmc_.tZR8lu5ydvjbwH9yTrYdAO6IRtM04v31P-lGsnLMk0M" width="20%">

In 130BC, **Hipparchus** was looking at the stars and comparing them with their positions 100 years in the past, and discovered that the stars moved at least **1° every century.**

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702675-9eed7081-3940-404c-8944-3978aa798e18.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQ3MDcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDQwNywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyNjc1LTllZWQ3MDgxLTM5NDAtNDA0Yy04OTQ0LTM5NzhhYTc5OGUxOC5wbmc_.RePy53qg713RW6f9QUzC-2HGO5r5YrX_prtMVm67RPA" width="60%">

Since the Earth rotates on its axis, it experiences a **greater outward force at the equator** due to its **greater acceleration**. The circumference of the Earth is **42km greater** at the equator for this reason. Since the Earth isn’t perfectly spherical, some parts of it which are more massive **experience a greater gravitational pull** from the Sun than others, causing the axis to wobble/spin. One revolution of the axis takes **26,000 years.**

He also found that the tropical year, which is determined by the time between spring equinoxes, is **20 minutes shorter** than the sidereal year (time taken for the Earth to return to the same position relative to a certain star). This is how he concluded that the Earth’s axis was wobbling. It is for this reason that our current **North Star**, Polaris, will change to be Vega in 12,000 years.

### Deflection and the Coriolis Effect

In 1632, **Galileo** claimed that since all stationary objects on the Earth’s surface have the same velocity as the surface itself and as the Earth is spinning **anticlockwise/eastward**, if an object was dropped from a very tall tower, it would theoretically land **slightly east** of its starting point, as the top of the tower would be moving faster than the surface of the Earth.  Due to **inertia**, when the object is dropped from the tower, it **maintains its higher velocity relative to the surface**, and since the Earth is rotating west to east, the object lands east of the tower. This is called **deflection.**

However, he argued that this effect would be negligible, using the lack of visible deflection to support his theory that motion shared by the Earth is imperceptible to observers on it.

<img src="https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcTG2fUmVi0MRO7rwNV_XqRVEQRpV8eTyGIwvG-TSKMylA&s" width="50%">

The same applies at the equator, as it has a greater velocity than the poles, therefore an object moving **away** from the equator will **experience deflection east** and an object moving **towards** the equator will **experience deflection west**. This is the reason for the **westerlies** and the **easterly trade winds.**

<img src="https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/189539911/552702822-8cacdd91-5155-428b-9ec9-4a3d360bb402.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3NzE1OTQ3MDcsIm5iZiI6MTc3MTU5NDQwNywicGF0aCI6Ii8xODk1Mzk5MTEvNTUyNzAyODIyLThjYWNkZDkxLTUxNTUtNDI4Yi05ZWM5LTRhM2QzNjBiYjQwMi5wbmc_.sfgUnuvoXDo6yS9fx580Z4nThBHpZousBJew0UX4-Yc" width="50%">

A great visualisation of the Coriolis effect is **Foucault’s pendulum.** It swings in a **straight line** due to inertia, but since the Earth is rotating beneath it, it appears as if the pendulum is slowly rotating.
